135.bp: E-commerce companies run dozens of marketing campaigns — banner ads, seasonal promotions, influencer collaborations — but measuring which ones actually drove sales is nearly impossible because a campaign uses vague creative language ("Summer Vibes Collection") while the sales database records concrete product purchases. This mismatch makes it impossible to train smarter campaign systems that learn which campaigns work for which audiences.
135.wh: The core problem is semantic ambiguity: a campaign about "adventure gear" might be promoting hiking boots, backpacks, or jackets, and a customer who bought a tent might have been influenced by the campaign or might have wanted it anyway. You can't just scan the campaign text for product keywords because marketing deliberately uses evocative, thematic language that doesn't directly name products. Without ground-truth labels saying "this customer bought this product because of this campaign," you're stuck with no training signal.

You can't just scan the campaign text for product keywords because marketing deliberately uses evocative, thematic language that doesn't directly name products. Without ground-truth labels saying "this customer bought this product because of this campaign," you're stuck with no training signal.
135.ap: The paper proposes a three-step pipeline: first, use an LLM to read the campaign creative and extract what product types it's actually selling (e.g., "Summer Vibes" implies clothing and accessories). Second, search the store's product taxonomy for all items matching those types. Third, have the LLM score each candidate product type to decide which ones the campaign genuinely promotes. Once you know what product types a campaign targets, any customer who bought from those types after seeing the campaign becomes a positive training example.
135.ww: This works because LLMs understand semantic intent in human language — they can parse marketing copy and extract the underlying product categories without needing exact keyword matches. By reframing the problem from "which exact products?" to "which product categories?" you move from an impossible matching problem to a tractable classification task. The approach generates high-confidence training labels automatically, so instead of hiring humans to annotate thousands of campaigns, the system annotates itself and learns to optimize campaign placement.
135.po: The method achieves 78–90% precision on internally validated campaign-to-product mappings, which means downstream ranking models can be trained with high-quality automatic labels. This unlocks the ability to build machine-learning systems that learn which types of campaigns drive which types of sales, enabling e-commerce platforms to automate campaign placement and improve return on ad spend at scale.

136.bp: Companies like Google deploy multi-agent systems where dozens of specialized AI components collaborate to answer user questions — one agent searches, one ranks, one scores relevance, one re-writes output. Designing how these agents should connect and talk to each other is done by hand, but the optimal topology changes depending on the question. A web search for "coffee recipes" needs different agent paths than a search for "medical symptoms."
136.wh: Today, engineers build separate model-and-topology pairs for each type of query domain, so you'd train one collaboration graph for shopping queries, another for academic research, another for health topics. This works poorly on novel domains and wastes work because fundamentally similar patterns (like "retrieve then rank") get learned from scratch each time. The ideal system should learn a universal understanding of topology and adapt it on the fly based on any new query.
136.ap: The paper presents a system that learns to generate agent-topology diagrams directly from a user's natural-language question. It uses two main ideas: a task-aware encoder that filters which agent information matters for a specific question (via sparse gating, essentially focusing attention on relevant signals), and a mixture-of-experts layer that selects different specialized sub-networks depending on the task type. The system is trained in three stages: first on canonical topologies to learn structural patterns, then on LLM-generated task-topology pairs to learn mappings from question types to graphs, finally fine-tuned on real systems.
136.ww: This works because task understanding and topology generation are mechanically separable — the question type (shopping vs. health) can be encoded once, then different specialized sub-networks can be activated to predict the right collaboration graph. By training on massive synthetic data (LLM-generated task-topology pairs), the model learns generalizable structural patterns that transfer to unseen domains. The key insight is that topology generation is learnable and domain-transferable, not something that must be hand-designed per task.
136.po: The system handles six diverse benchmark domains in experiments using a single model, eliminating the need to train separate models for each query type. This reduces engineering overhead and enables dynamic adaptation: when a novel query type appears, the system predicts the optimal agent topology instead of requiring manual redesign, making multi-agent systems more practical to deploy in production services like search engines.

137.bp: Imagine hospitals in different cities clustering their patient records to find disease patterns, or banks clustering transaction networks to detect fraud rings — except data privacy laws mean each organization keeps its data on its own servers and can't share raw information. Federated clustering solves this by letting them collaborate to find patterns without exposing private data.
137.wh: The standard clustering trick is to ask all agents to find the same number of clusters, but in reality, one hospital might discover three disease subtypes while another discovers five because their patient populations are genuinely different. When the server tries to merge cluster results from clients with different numbers of clusters, it fails because there's no clear way to align clusters across heterogeneous groupings. Raw averaging produces gibberish — you'd be averaging a 3-cluster result with a 5-cluster result, losing structure.
137.ap: The paper proposes splitting each client's data into public and private components: public information (cluster-level summaries that are safe to share) gets sent to the server in anonymized form, while private information (the detailed raw data) stays local. Clients with different cluster numbers can now coexist because they only exchange cluster prototypes, not raw data. On the server, cluster prototypes are aligned by computing similarity between them, so clients with 3 clusters and 5 clusters can agree on shared structure despite different granularities.
137.ww: By decoupling public (sharable) and private (local) data, the system sidesteps the alignment problem. Cluster prototypes are abstract summaries that can be compared even when they represent different partitions of the same underlying domain. The server computes prototype affinity (how similar different clusters are) to find the natural shared structure. This allows federated learning without forcing everyone into the same structure.
137.po: The method achieves privacy-preserving graph clustering across heterogeneous clients where each can choose its own number of clusters. Experiments show it prevents performance degradation that occurs when you naively average results from clients with mismatched cluster counts, making federated clustering practical for decentralized applications like multi-hospital disease discovery or multi-bank fraud detection.

138.bp: When rumors or fake news spreads on social media, platforms need to find the original source account so they can take action. Given a snapshot of who has seen or shared a rumor, the challenge is to trace back and identify patient zero — the account that started it all.
138.wh: Deep-learning methods sound like they'd be great for this, but they stumble on three problems. First, they layer on so many feature engineering tricks (special embeddings for cascades, auxiliary attention layers, metadata enrichment) that the models become huge, and you can't afford to retrain when a new rumor emerges. Second, real-world misinformation cascades are rare, so people simulate artificial cascades for training, but artificial spreading patterns don't match reality and the model falls apart. Third, retraining the full model for every new rumor is too slow for real-time deployment.
138.ap: Instead of building a heavyweight deep model, the paper takes inspiration from prompt-learning (the idea that pre-trained models can adapt to new tasks with minimal data). It pre-trains a lightweight classifier on adaptive subgraphs centered around the rumor source, using artificially generated cascades only for this pre-training phase. Then at test time, instead of retraining, it prompts the model with just a few examples of the current rumor's spreading pattern and asks it to localize the source. The prompting approach sidesteps both model bloat and the need to retrain on every new cascade.
138.ww: This works because source localization has a consistent geometric structure — infected nodes cluster around the true source — so a model trained on that structure (even via simulation) can recognize it in real data. By treating inference as a prompt-answering task rather than a model-retraining task, the system stays lightweight and fast. The key insight is that you don't need to refit the model per cascade; you can pre-learn the structural signature and prompt it at test time.
138.po: The method achieves both parameter efficiency and speed: it's a lightweight model that doesn't explode in size, and it can localize rumor sources in seconds without retraining, making real-time deployment feasible. It also handles the low-data regime better than deep methods because prompting works with few examples, so the annotation gap (scarcity of real cascades) becomes less of a bottleneck.

139.bp: Banks need to forecast the demand for multiple types of transactions (checking, savings, loans) across different branches over the next hour. Weather services need to predict wind speed and temperature simultaneously. Time-series forecasting is everywhere in real services, but current large-scale models centralize data from all branches or regions into one place for training, raising privacy and governance concerns.
139.wh: Federated time-series forecasting faces two interconnected problems: different clients have different numbers of variables (one branch tracks 5 types of transactions, another tracks 10), and these variables exhibit different temporal patterns (one might see daily cycles, another weekly). A model trained on one client's data doesn't transfer to another because both the variable structure and the time-dependent patterns are heterogeneous, so you can't just average model weights across federated clients.
139.ap: The paper proposes a two-pathway architecture for each client: a global pathway that learns common low-frequency patterns (slow, smooth trends shared across all clients) and a local pathway that learns personalized high-frequency patterns (spikes, noise, client-specific variations). These two paths are kept separate during training using frequency-aware loss functions that explicitly push low-frequency components to the global path and high-frequency residuals to the local path. A gated fusion mechanism then combines both paths at prediction time for the final forecast.
139.ww: By decomposing the forecasting problem into frequency bands, the system exploits a natural structure in time series: most information lives in different frequency ranges depending on client and variable. Low frequencies generalize across clients (shared trends), while high frequencies are heterogeneous (client-specific noise and spikes). Separating them during training means the global path can learn shared structure and be safely averaged, while local paths stay personalized. At test time, the fusion gate learns to weight them appropriately.
139.po: The method enables privacy-preserving time-series forecasting where each client keeps its data local but benefits from shared learning of common temporal patterns. Extensive experiments show it outperforms existing federated approaches on forecasting benchmarks with heterogeneous variables and temporal correlations, making multi-branch and multi-region forecasting practical without centralizing sensitive data.

140.bp: Recommendation systems suggest movies, products, or songs by modeling the geometry of user preferences — if user A likes movies 1, 2, 3 and user B likes movies 2, 3, 4, then A and B probably have similar tastes and can recommend movies to each other. The challenge is that user-item interaction graphs have wildly different local structures in different parts: some users form tight clusters (niche tastes), others scatter widely (broad tastes).
140.wh: Existing methods assume the entire graph sits in one uniform geometric space, like a flat plane where distance means similarity everywhere. But this assumption is wrong: some users cluster densely (tight taste communities) while others distribute sparsely (diverse individual preferences), and a single fixed geometry can't capture both. If you use a space where similar users cluster well, you'll distort sparse regions, and vice versa.
140.ap: The paper reframes recommendation as a physical process evolving on a curved, time-varying manifold (using Hamiltonian dynamics, an idea from physics). Instead of assuming a fixed geometry, it learns a node-dependent Riemannian metric — essentially a custom shape of space around each user and item that reflects local topology. Information propagates along these curved, adaptive surfaces rather than through linear tangent-space approximations. The channel-wise metric captures that different features might need different geometries too.
140.ww: This works because graphs with topological heterogeneity (dense clusters and sparse regions) naturally live on curved spaces where the geometry is locally adaptive. By learning the metric (the shape of space) rather than fixing it, the model can have tight clustering where appropriate and loose spreading where appropriate. The Hamiltonian approach ensures that information propagates correctly on these curved surfaces without geometric distortion. The paper proves this dynamics has a unique stable solution.
140.po: Experiments show consistent improvements over baseline methods on five benchmarks for recommendation tasks. The adaptive geometric approach captures long-range dependencies better than fixed-geometry methods, so users discover recommendations from farther parts of the graph, and the method handles both tight clusters and diffuse regions without sacrificing either.

141.bp: Pathologists examine tissue slides under microscopes to spot cancer and other diseases, looking at tiny morphological details (cell arrangement, texture, color shifts). Modern AI can help, but the issue is that these AI models are trained on massive slide datasets, and applying them to a new hospital with different slide-staining protocols or scanner equipment requires retraining, which is slow and expensive.
141.wh: Vision-Language models (like image and text foundation models) promise to solve this by leveraging semantic knowledge: you can describe an anomaly in words and the model can find it visually. But there's a granularity mismatch: pathology abnormalities are tiny local features (a specific region's cell clustering), while these large pre-trained models were trained on whole-image-level concepts. The model's generic visual understanding misses the fine detail, and semantic descriptions don't ground in the specific spatial context of that particular region-of-interest.
141.ap: The paper proposes a hierarchical alignment mechanism: visual features from the tissue sample first ground text prompts, generating content-adaptive descriptions that are specific to that slide. Then these description-grounded prompts guide the visual encoder back to spotlight where anomalies are. The process alternates: vision informs language, language refines vision. A dual-branch inference strategy at test time combines semantic scores (model confidence) with geometric prototypes (actual tissue statistics) to stabilize predictions in few-shot settings where there's minimal training data.
141.ww: By enforcing a communication loop between vision and language, the model ensures that semantic concepts are anchored in the specific visual context of each slide. This solves the granularity mismatch because language provides semantic understanding but vision grounds it spatially. The dual-branch approach hedges: semantic scores capture conceptual knowledge, geometric prototypes capture real tissue statistics, and combining both prevents overfitting when data is scarce.
141.po: The method outperforms existing approaches across four benchmark datasets for pathology anomaly detection with limited data. It effectively adapts Vision-Language models to the fine-grained needs of pathology, enabling hospitals to deploy AI diagnostic aids even with small domain-specific training datasets, reducing the need for large centralized annotated collections.

142.bp: Large language models (LLMs) are remarkably good at reasoning over text, but they can't natively work with graphs (social networks, knowledge bases, scientific citation networks). The goal is to tokenize graphs — convert them into sequences of tokens that LLMs can process — so we can ask an LLM questions about a graph and get coherent answers.
142.wh: Current approaches convert graphs into token sequences but lose critical information: they rely only on text prompts and descriptions to guide the LLM, creating a text-biased alignment where the model understands the linguistic description but ignores the actual graph structure. The LLM learns what words mean but doesn't deeply encode graph connectivity, so it can't truly reason about graph structure — it's mimicking text understanding, not graph understanding.
142.ap: The paper proposes explicitly reconstructing the graph from the LLM's tokenized output as an additional training signal. During instruction-tuning (the process of teaching an LLM to follow commands), instead of only matching text descriptions, the model also tries to predict the graph's structure from its own token representations. This reconstruction task forces the LLM to encode graph information directly into its tokens, not just text semantics. The paper proves information-theoretically that this reconstruction objective tightens the alignment between graphs and the model's internal representations.
142.ww: By adding graph reconstruction as a loss function, the training process explicitly penalizes the model if it encodes text semantics but ignores graph structure. The model must learn to encode both: what the graph's text descriptions mean (semantic alignment) and what the graph's connections are (structural alignment). The information-theoretic bound shows this is optimal: the best graph-text alignment is upper-bounded by how much of the graph's information makes it into the model's hidden states.
142.po: The RGLM framework improves alignment between graphs and LLMs beyond text-only approaches, enabling the LLM to perform better on graph reasoning tasks like link prediction, node classification, and retrieval over graphs. This is a step toward building truly universal LLMs that handle both text and structured data, moving beyond the current paradigm where LLMs are great at language but see graphs as mere text descriptions.

143.bp: Lawyers and compliance teams perform high-recall document review: scanning thousands of emails to find all documents relevant to a legal case (goal: find 90–95% of responsive documents). Time and budget are limited, so they need to know when to stop reviewing — but without reading every single remaining document, it's impossible to know how many responsive documents they've missed.
143.wh: The core tension is that recall is invisible: you can't measure how many responsive documents you missed without looking at everything, but looking at everything defeats the purpose. Current methods either use statistical sampling (expensive and slow) or trust the ranking model (which might miss rare relevant documents). The standard stopping rules require either exhaustive review or costly estimation.
143.ap: The paper develops two statistical approaches that combine information from a document ranker (a machine-learning model that scores how likely each document is responsive) and a small random sample of documents. The Bayesian approach treats the ranker's scores as an informative prior belief about responsiveness, then updates it with what the random sample reveals. The model-assisted approach (generalized regression estimator) uses the ranker's calibrated probabilities as anchors and adjusts them based on sampling bias correction, following design-based statistics principles. Both produce lower-bound estimates of recall that are conservative — they underestimate rather than overestimate.
143.ww: This works because the ranker has signal (it's better than random at identifying relevant documents) but isn't perfect, and the random sample provides unbiased ground truth. Combining them leverages the ranker's strength (speed, coverage) while using the sample to correct its blind spots. The Bayesian framing is intuitive: update your belief (ranker scores) with new evidence (sample), while the model-assisted framing follows statistical best practices by accounting for sampling design. Conservative estimates protect against accidentally stopping too early.
143.po: The framework enables legal and compliance teams to estimate true recall early in the review process using practical stopping rules, reducing the cost and time of high-recall document review. Instead of reviewing until exhaustion or relying on hunches, reviewers can make statistically grounded decisions about when to stop, balancing confidence in recall against review costs.

144.bp: When an LLM answers a user's question, it often needs to cite facts from a knowledge base (a company's internal documents, recent news, Wikipedia). The challenge is retrieving the right passages from millions of documents — you can't use the whole knowledge base because that would give the LLM too much context and slow everything down.
144.wh: Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems search for documents using semantic similarity to the question, but they typically retrieve shallow subgraphs (just nearby nodes in a document graph) or use pre-computed communities that don't adapt to the specific question. A question about "how does insulin regulate blood sugar in diabetic patients?" might need facts about hormone mechanisms, glucose metabolism, and disease pathways — concepts that are related in complex ways in a knowledge graph, not just nearby neighbors.
144.ap: The paper proposes using attributed community search — a graph algorithm that dynamically extracts relevant subgraphs based on the query. Given a question, the system finds communities (dense clusters of related concepts) in the knowledge graph that are topically relevant. Unlike pre-computed communities (which are static), these are extracted on the fly based on the query's intent. The system adds a chunk-level graph index, allowing multi-granularity retrieval: you can retrieve at the document level, the paragraph level, or the fact level, depending on what's needed.
144.ww: By searching for dynamic communities rather than pre-computed ones, the system adapts to specific queries and captures higher-order structure (multi-hop relationships) that simple semantic search misses. The chunk-level index enables efficiency: instead of indexing every fact independently, you group facts into chunks and retrieve chunks, reducing index size and token overhead. This is faster and cheaper than alternatives while maintaining retrieval quality.
144.po: On multiple benchmark datasets, DA-RAG outperforms existing graph-based RAG methods by up to 40%, while also reducing index construction time and token overhead by 37–41%. This means more accurate answers from LLMs using less computational cost, making LLM-based search engines more practical for production deployment.

145.bp: Data has become a tradeable commodity: companies buy training data, market data, sensor data, and customer behavior data to improve their products and services. But how should data be priced? A dataset's value depends on how much it improves predictions for each buyer, and different buyers value the same data differently based on what they already know.
145.wh: Traditional pricing assumes goods are rivalrous (if I buy something, you can't) and thus uses supply-and-demand curves. Data is non-rival: I can sell the same dataset to you and to a thousand other companies simultaneously. Standard market equilibrium concepts don't directly apply because prices need to coordinate the simultaneous allocation of the same data to multiple buyers, each with different utility functions for prediction improvement.
145.ap: The paper adapts competitive equilibrium — a foundational economic concept for pricing rivalrous goods — to data markets by modifying the market-clearing condition. Instead of requiring that supply equals demand (impossible for non-rival goods), it allows the same data to be allocated to multiple buyers. Each buyer's utility function explicitly models how purchasing data improves their predictive performance (not just "I want more stuff"). The paper proves that equilibrium always exists and is typically unique and rational (prices are finite and meaningful).
145.ww: This works because even though data is non-rival, scarcity still exists: the seller has limited data, and selling to one buyer doesn't preclude selling to others, so prices should reflect the value data provides to each buyer's prediction task. By embedding prediction improvement directly into utility functions, the model captures what actually matters: how much each buyer is willing to pay depends on how much their model accuracy improves. Competitive equilibrium finds a price vector where supply and demand are balanced accounting for this real value.
145.po: The framework opens a path toward principled pricing in data markets: a single-price vector can simultaneously satisfy all buyers and the seller. The paper designs an algorithm to find approximate equilibria efficiently despite the non-convexity of the pricing landscape, enabling practical data marketplaces where data is priced based on its utility for prediction rather than arbitrary haggling.

146.bp: Deepfakes—AI-generated fake videos—pose serious security risks: they can impersonate people, spread disinformation, and undermine trust in media. Detecting them is critical, but a detection system trained on deepfakes generated by one technique (e.g., face-swapping software) often fails when the technique changes (now using neural rendering, next year using diffusion models).
146.wh: Detection methods typically optimize for one goal: spot all forgeries with high accuracy. But deepfakes are diverse: some are created via face-swapping, others via lip-sync, others via expression manipulation, each leaving different telltale traces. Treating all fakes as a single "Fake" category means the model learns a generic fraud signal instead of understanding the specific characteristics of each forgery method. When a new technique appears, the model fails because it learned the wrong patterns.
146.ap: The paper proposes decomposing detection into two separate subspaces: a semantic subspace (what the content is about — a person, a scene) and a forgery subspace (how the fake was created). It uses orthogonal decomposition — a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique where you project learned features onto orthogonal directions that isolate forgery patterns from semantic patterns. It further breaks the "Fake" category into sub-categories corresponding to different deepfake generation techniques and learns a manifold representation for each, using a sparsely-gated mixture structure to activate the right sub-model per technique.
146.ww: By separating semantic and forgery subspaces, the model avoids conflating content (which varies) with creation technique (which is the actual signal). Orthogonal decomposition ensures these subspaces don't interfere. Breaking fakes into technique-specific sub-categories means each sub-model learns precise signals for one technique, and when a new technique appears, the mixture can theoretically extend or interpolate. The gating mechanism activates the right detector per technique, improving generalization.
146.po: Experiments across six real-world deepfake detection datasets with multiple evaluation protocols show leading performance. By modeling semantic and forgery subspaces separately and specializing per generation technique, the method generalizes better across datasets and is more robust to emerging deepfake methods, advancing the security posture of platforms vulnerable to video manipulation.

147.bp: WebAssembly lets companies run C and C++ programs in web browsers safely, enabling applications like PDF viewers and image editors to run client-side. But WebAssembly's memory model is monolithic — all data (stack, heap, global variables) lives in one big linear block. A buffer overflow in one part of the program can corrupt memory anywhere else, creating serious security holes.
147.wh: Current defenses require either source code (to add explicit checks), specialized runtime engines (slower and not standard), or heavyweight binary instrumentation that adds millions of extra instructions and slows programs down significantly. Commercial off-the-shelf WebAssembly binaries don't come with source code and are compiled for standard runtimes, so existing approaches don't apply.
147.ap: The paper presents Bento, a static binary rewriter that takes compiled WebAssembly and rewrites it without needing source code. It analyzes all pointer uses in the entire program to partition memory into logical regions: the stack, the heap, and global data. It then rewrites memory accesses to map each region to an isolated instance using WebAssembly's multi-memory feature (a standard capability). This creates a software-based memory management unit where each region is isolated, preventing overflow in one from corrupting another.
147.ww: This works because WebAssembly's multi-memory feature provides native isolation at no cost — accessing an isolated memory region is just a different index, not an extra instruction. By analyzing the whole program's pointer usage, Bento determines what region each memory access targets, then rewrites accesses to use the correct isolated instance. The key insight is that static analysis can determine memory region partitioning automatically, and hardware-native isolation is free.
147.po: Bento successfully mitigates real-world attacks in production applications like Libpng and PDFAlto with only 3% runtime slowdown and 1% startup overhead, while preserving program semantics. This enables deployment of memory-safe WebAssembly in browsers without recompilation, specialized runtimes, or source code access, significantly improving security of in-browser native-code applications.

148.bp: Modern vehicles have powerful battery systems with dozens of electrical loads—heaters, air conditioning, infotainment systems, charging ports. The battery management system needs to predict demand for the next few minutes to optimize battery health and avoid failures. But driver behavior is unpredictable: the same person might use the heater in the morning and air conditioning in the afternoon.
148.wh: Predicting electrical load is hard because demand depends on driver behavior, which seems random over short timescales. Standard statistical models treat each prediction independently, assuming past load is irrelevant. But in reality, there's hidden structure: if the driver just turned on the heater, they're likely to keep it on for several minutes. Short-term history contains predictive signal that naive models ignore.
148.ap: The paper analyzes the public vehicle dataset (VED) and shows that including the past 60 seconds of electrical load history (heater power, air conditioner power, etc.) and computing conditional probability distributions based on that history improves prediction. Instead of a single prediction for the next moment, you compute how likely different load levels are given the recent pattern. For high-load scenarios (when drivers are actively using multiple systems), incorporating this history reduces prediction variance by up to 41.7%, meaning more accurate and stable estimates.
148.ww: Short-term history contains state information about driver intent: if the heater is on now, the driver is probably cold and will keep it on. Conditional probability distributions capture this: what's the distribution of next-load given current-load? This structure is learnable from historical data. When validated with a LightGBM model (a fast machine-learning algorithm), the conditional-history approach tracks rapid load changes better than simpler statistical methods.
148.po: By incorporating 60 seconds of power history, prediction uncertainty drops significantly during high-load periods when reliability matters most. This enables more precise battery management in software-defined vehicles, improving battery longevity and preventing unexpected power failures in demanding conditions like extreme heat or cold.

149.bp: Social platforms like Facebook and financial systems like PayPal face relentless attacks from bad actors: scammers orchestrating fake-promotion schemes, fraudsters running account-takeover rings, money launderers creating shell accounts. These illicit accounts often hide among millions of legitimate ones by mimicking normal behavior on the surface.
149.wh: The standard approach is binary classification (legitimate or fraudulent) based on user profile features like age, follower count, or account age. But illicit accounts are sophisticated — a scammer might genuinely add friends, post normal-looking content, and initiate small transactions, perfectly mimicking benign users on the surface. However, the pattern and context of behaviors differ: a legitimate user adds friends to connect, a fraudster adds friends to build a network for the scam. The same action has different purposes, so you can't detect fraud from actions alone.
149.ap: The paper proposes detecting fraud from behavior sequences rather than static profiles. It extracts two types of behavior patterns: category-specific patterns (what sequences do legitimate users form? what sequences do scammers form?) and contextualized action encoding (how do the same actions mean different things in different contexts?). The framework uses pattern mining to discover common behavior subsequences within each user type, then aligns action sequences with context (what other actions happen before/after). It fuses the mined patterns with context-aware encodings into a unified detection model.
149.ww: Behavior sequences contain temporal structure that static profiles miss: a legitimate user following a friend after receiving a message looks different from a fraudster building a network. By mining category-specific patterns, the model learns what legitimate sequences look like and what fraudster sequences look like. Contextualized encoding means the same action ("add friend") gets encoded differently depending on surrounding context. Patterns provide structure (templates of normal vs. illicit behavior), context provides grounding (what the action means in this situation).
149.po: The PIAD framework improves detection of diverse illicit account types (scammers, fake promoters, money launderers) by modeling their distinct behavioral signatures. By focusing on behavior sequences and context rather than static features, the method catches sophisticated fraud that mimics surface legitimacy, enabling platforms to protect users against coordinated attacks.
